stories.title: I'm not. Honest.
stories.author: David Wiles
stories.transcript:
I visited an old friend the other day. He knows I have a 3D printer and asked if I could help him make something. I asked what it was. He said it was an eagle — a reproduction of something he’d seen at an auction. He’d thought about buying it at the time but decided against it, and now regretted it.
I asked what kind of eagle it was. I had a pretty good idea, but I wanted him to say it.
It was a Nazi eagle, with, as he described it, “a great big swastika underneath”.
I asked him why he wanted it. He quickly said he “wasn’t a Nazi” and that he “just liked the look of things like that”.
He then started talking about other Nazi artefacts he’d seen and collected, and, perhaps sensing that I wasn’t entirely convinced, began listing their supposed values, as if the price tags somehow justified the interest.
I said it would probably be possible to make something similar, but he’d have to finish it himself with gold leaf or foil to make it look like metal. I had a quick look online for free CAD models of anything suitable. The results were exactly what you’d expect.
I have no intention of making it.
At that point I put on my best dark, ominous voice and repeatedly told him: “You must look deep down inside yourself and ask yourself why you like these things.”
He wasn’t impressed.
Trying to lift the mood, I asked where he was planning to put it once it was finished.
“On the wall, to the right of the chimney breast there,” he said, pointing with his right arm raised.
“Perfect,” I said. “You could put a portrait of the Führer on the other side.”
Without missing a beat, he replied: “Oh, I’ve got a bust of him down there.”
He pointed.
I looked.
“It’s not an original,” he added.

stories.title: Basket case
stories.author: David Wiles
stories.transcript:
When I was a child and ill off school, I used to wave my mother off on her way to the shop from a comfy chair in the sun.
I can see her now, in my mind, through windows long gone, proud as punch, strutting off, hair up, eyes down; setting herself like a duck at thunder. 
She’d turn, smile and give me a little wave with one free hand. On her other arm, a fine wicker basket.
I often examined this thing, trying to follow the mazelike woven twists and turns of its makeup; searching for where it all began and where it all ended.
It creaked when you squeezed it, and it had a natural smell. A bit like me.
I’m not sure if it’s still kicking around. I should have a look.
When I was living and working in London, during  a trip back up north, I noticed that my dad had bought some red plastic shopping baskets for general use.
Whenever they went shopping, one would be put in the car.
I think they had been bought from the now-deceased Wilko. They were quite similar to the ones actually used in the shops. Whoever had the brainwave in Wilko to start selling these lookalike baskets, I don’t think had really thought it through.
On many occasions when I was out with them, my dad would get challenged at checkout by staff who would tell him that he couldn’t take the basket. You could see he was sick of it.
I wonder if they’d maybe had so many pinched that they decided that partial privatisation of their public infrastructure was perhaps the way forward. Who knows. Neither Wilko nor Thatcher are available for comment.
When Dad died, I found two of these baskets in the house. I was now looking after Mum and helping her with shopping.
I started using one of those red baskets when I went out with her.
After a while, wherever I went, I was usually carrying something to do with whatever project I was engaged in, along with various sets of keys, phone etc. So the basket just made itself very useful.
By the time I had to put Mum in a care home, it had become part of my daily life.
One night I was out in the pub when Anne, a friendly, flirty woman, who worked at the care home, sidled up to me and told me something revealing.
She said that another member of staff, Lauren, fancied me.
I replied sternly that Lauren was married and had two kids.
Anne said that this didn’t really matter “these days”.
I said that I thought it did.
At the end of the conversation, she gave me some advice.
“Dave: Ditch the basket.”
I had it with me at the time. I looked at it, there on the floor of the pub next to my feet, and thought. Nah: Way too useful.
Of the two baskets, which must now be twenty years old, one has died. I used it too many times to propel myself from kneeling to standing, and it collapsed under my weight.
The second one is just about to fail. We never learn.
When I was in B&Q recently, I saw they had some stout black ones next to their trolleys for use in the shop. I wasn’t tempted to pinch one; they’re tagged and, well; you know.
I looked underneath one to see if there was a maker’s name in the moulding. There was, so I photographed it and looked online for the manufacturer when I got home.
I emailed them; a company in Stalybridge. I got a polite reply back and was sent a link to an online shop.
I noticed that they were available in different colours. This is important. To avoid being accused of basket theft, you need to pick a colour which is not going to alert the attention of excitable shop staff.
I chose yellow.
I couldn’t think of any major retailer in the UK which has yellow as a main brand colour.
I ordered three. I know they will be useful. I can leave one in the car, take one to London and have the other for any ongoing job I’m working on.
A week went by. No baskets. I rang them up. They said that the courier had told them that they’d tried, but failed, to deliver and that card notifications had been put through the door. I said that I hadn’t seen any cards.
They said they would look into it.
Another fortnight went by. Still no baskets.
More conversations. Still no baskets.
I saw Anne recently down the street. She looked down at my basket and then looked back at me with one eyebrow slightly raised. 
I said I knew that it was looking a bit worse for wear and that I’d ordered a replacement. 
She nodded.
I told her about the delivery cock-ups. 
She nodded. 
I asked her if she had maybe intercepted my communications with the basket supplier to wean me off them. 
She laughed and said that Lauren had left her husband.
The baskets arrived yesterday.

stories.title: The Callous
stories.author: David Wiles
stories.transcript:
I have been visiting two elderly, close-neighbour friends quite frequently over the past couple of weeks.
They are a couple in their 80s. Ann is now very ill, extremely weak and bed-bound. She has been in and out of hospital since suffering a small stroke and a fall two months ago.
Roy, her husband, is palpably annoyed with her and with the whole situation. He genuinely resents the impact her illness has had on his life. He complains that it has been going on for at least 20 years.
A couple of years ago, Roy signed up with Age Concern as a volunteer visitor to other isolated elderly people. Yet he constantly complains about the people he visits. It is obvious that he has very little understanding of dementia, and he is particularly irritated by the man he visits. The man cannot help having dementia. I don’t understand why Roy does it. He is clearly not suited to the role.
Two days ago, I mentioned to Roy that I had some foot problems. He suggested that I give Emma, their chiropodist, a call. I told him I already had, but hadn’t received a reply. I know she is usually very busy; on one occasion I had to wait six weeks to see her.
Roy mentioned that Emma was coming to them on 12 September. I remember thinking that was still a few weeks away, but I thought I could put up with the pain until then.
I rang Emma again yesterday and left a message. I mentioned that Roy had told me she was visiting them on 12 September and asked whether she might be able to pop across and do my feet afterwards.
She normally does Ann and Roy’s feet together, so I assumed she would probably be able to fit me in afterwards, particularly as Ann will almost certainly have died by next week.

stories.title: Reparations
stories.author: David Wiles
stories.transcript:
The global pandemic was, overwhelmingly, a bad thing. But there were a few positives.

Wildlife had an opportunity to just get on with it. There were some extraordinary advances in medicine and medical technology. Lidl was mostly empty after 9:30 PM.

For me, as a chatterbox, the pandemic provided a great opportunity to revive old friendships on the telephone. 

Some had faded away many years ago; others had always been there, but had become less frequent. All needed a little attention.

I’ve built three of those friendships into ongoing conversations, with instalments every few days. The others are still there, too.

Some of those conversations exposed political leanings in friends I hadn’t been aware of when I was younger. 

I just wasn’t politically motivated then and, I suppose, neither were they. 

We all take different paths.

Some of us just weren’t on the same frequency at all. There were some heated exchanges, which threatened to spoil our friendships. But we kind of got over ourselves, re-established boundaries, patched up the holes and soldiered on.

Life’s too short.

I think a big part of my political journey was shaped by my involvement on the fringes of Blacktivism.

My dear old friend and erstwhile partner, Jean, is mixed race. 

Having an immigrant mum from the Caribbean and a dad from South East London made her childhood complicated. 

Poor mental health has also been a severe and continuing battle she has courageously struggled with.

During the pandemic, she began to think about her Blackness and how she could connect with it. She was trying to find somewhere to be, as a mixed-race kid who had been brought up in a white, middle-class suburb.

She joined several Windrush justice campaign groups, national and international reparations groups, and threw herself into the world of extended Zoom calls.

I was on the fringes of this, often looking over her shoulder or joining remotely. I never contributed. I just observed.

I enjoyed myself. It was a fascinating place to inhabit.

I was jokingly introduced as one of the “Wazungu” and gradually got to know some of the hardened activists in those groups.

I wouldn’t say these zoom calls were overly objective, capable or ever so friendly. They could often be very chaotic. How could they be anything else, as huge committees, with hundreds of participants from all corners of the world?

But they were an education, and it made me think a lot about the impact of the Transatlantic Slave Trade and the history of European imperialism.

While I’m not an expert, I’m sceptical of those who tell me that the so-called historical eras of “discovery” and “empire” were nuanced.

Goal-driven humans can be remarkably ruthless when pursuing what they want, particularly when they believe no one with greater moral authority is looking. There’s not so much nuance here.

The word nuance is itself a French loanword, entering English in the late eighteenth century.

I sometimes wonder about words like this, and if their role is to make ugly things sound more intellectually respectable.

French became the language of the ruling elite in England after the Normans invaded in 1066. There’s still a lot of French woven into English law. French is still viewed in Britain as sophisticated. Likely by people who also purport to hate the French.

Specialised language can be a useful way of simplifying complex things for discussion. But it can also be a way of excluding people from the discussion altogether.

“Nuance” and “Wazungu” are very different words, but perhaps they can sometimes do the same job: marking the boundary between those who understand the language and those who don’t.
At some point during all this, Jean managed to secure a BBC commission to make an hour-long documentary film. A bit of a leap, I know. But it’s relevant.

The film didn’t really have a concrete plan. Planning isn’t something Jean is particularly good at. I suspect the ADHD doesn’t help.

It got made and it got broadcast.

It turned out to be a wonderful autobiographical journey into what it means to be mixed race.

After its broadcast, Jean was invited to show her film at several film festivals and give Q&A sessions afterwards. 

One such event was the Barbados International Film Festival.

A friend and I decided we’d like to go along with Jean. We had to pay our own way, but managed to get two cheap return flights at very short notice.

It was great fun. The festival was quite a splendid affair and the film and Q&A was a great success.

Towards the end of that trip, in January 2024, we visited what the Bajan Government called an ‘Industrial Monument’.

I must admit, I said to my companions that it would be a bit of a waste of time, as there would likely be ‘nothing to see’ there.

There may not have been much to ‘see’, apart from some small information boards on stakes. But there was an awful lot to feel.

The ‘Industrial Monument’ was a former slave burial ground on what used to be the Newton Plantation.

A quiet, off-the-beaten-track corner of a field, on a gently sloping, grassy hillside.

Punctuated by a couple of trees at its centre, with some benches beneath them in the shade, there was a purposeful place you could sit and think.

It was a deeply emotional experience.

The information panels explained how the burial ground had been discovered, how it had undergone an archaeological survey in the early 1990s, and what that survey suggested about the burial practices of the enslaved African people who had lived and died there in the seventeenth, eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

Harrowing stuff.

The tree at its centre, a large, majestic Shack-Shack, is a common variety in the tropics. It was full of long, dried, browned, hanging seed pods, which, like percussion shakers, gently whispered in the wind.

On the ground, beneath the tree, there were scores of them.

All full of seeds.

I picked up a few. I had in mind that I would like to grow my own trees from these very seeds. Seeds from the tree whose roots were in the earth where hundreds of men, women and children had, after horrible, short lives, been laid to rest.

I secreted three full pods into my small backpack before the flight.

Very naughty, I know.

The trees are by me now.
In my studio.

They’re three-year-old shrubs, two metres tall, in pots, in the warm.

stories.title: Retail Therapy
stories.author: David Wiles
stories.transcript:
Ken first materialised at school one day in late September. We had already begun, as five-year-olds, on our education some weeks earlier.
I still have a good memory for detail, and I vividly remember seeing Ken for the first time that day. He had a dull yellow, crew-neck, chunky-knit jumper, short mid-brown hair and very dark brown eyes.
The teacher encouraged us to welcome him. He soon fitted right in and rubbed along with us all.
During the next year, Ken developed a really nasty problem with psoriasis. Quite quickly, his skin became very dry and scaly. His scalp became extremely scaly and his hair was constantly full of very large flakes of skin, tangled in it.
A lot of us used to make fun of him. We were undeniably cruel.
When I was eight, the class I was in was mixed with kids who were a year older because there was a shortage of classrooms and teachers. Rather than being disadvantageous, it was actually really enjoyable for me. A group of the older kids sort of took me under their wing.
It was the only time in my life when I enjoyed playing football. I wasn't very good at it, but those older kids really encouraged me, and I got quite a bit better with their support.
I remember once making jokes about Ken and his skin with them. He wasn't in that class, but everyone knew him.
One of the older kids told me off. Not in a bad way, but calmly. He explained why it was wrong to say things like that about Ken.
After that, I didn't say things like that about Ken again.
Ken was from a poor family. His mother was originally from a local village. She had been a nurse. While at work, she fell in love with one of her patients, a migrant worker.
They married and, relatively soon afterwards, emigrated to Australia. I think Ken and one of his sisters were born there.
For reasons I don't know, they returned to the UK when Ken was five and came to live in the town here.
When I was fourteen, I was doing O Levels. One was in Computer Studies. It was 1979, the beginning of the availability of cheap home computers.
A couple of maths teachers had an interest in the field and set up the course. I don't know what made me choose it as an option, but I'm glad I did.
In the first year of the O Level, we only had an old electro-mechanical teletype terminal. It was like a big, clacking automatic typewriter. The BBC used to feature one on Saturday's Grandstand when they showed the football results as they came in from Littlewoods Pools.
That machine in the school wasn't a computer. It was just a dumb terminal and had to be connected by telephone, through a rubber acoustic coupler, to a computer at the other end of a special line. It wasn't unlike the first internet modems: it used special audio signals to send and receive instructions.
The computer belonged to the local city authority across the river and was used for council work, including payrolls and traffic-light management.
The school had an agreement that gave us access for a few hours a week.
We loved that class.
In the second year, the school acquired several of the first desktop computers. We began to spend hours on these things after school, with little or no supervision. Mostly respectfully.
The new first-year O-Level group joined in, and we all got to know one another. Great fun.
It was around that time that I started to get friendly with Ken.
He still had an issue with psoriasis, but I didn't really see that any more. He was a nice person. Poor, but really nice.
I started inviting him to join us in the computer classroom after hours. I showed him how to write simple programs in BASIC.
One night, he'd been playing on the terminal and had typed something on it.
In class the next day, the teacher noticed what he'd left typed on the paper roll. It was something rude. I knew it was him and, without batting an eyelid, I shopped him to the teacher.
I don't know why I did it. I still regret it even now.
He got told off, and access to the computer after hours was shut down for a while.
I still remained friends with him, but we weren't so close after that.
Life for me as a teenager was pretty horrible. I didn't develop properly, physically and emotionally as a result. While most kids go through a rebellious phase, I sort of did too, but nothing bad. No delinquency.
My mother knew Ken's family and, although she didn't dislike them, she didn't really want me to play with Ken. She assumed Ken would be a bad influence on me.
My parents were from very working-class backgrounds and were enjoying a bit of new found money through Dad's decision to set up as a plumber on his own. They were aspiring to become middle class, and they wanted me to do well.
Ken's dad was German. He was also becoming a plumber, having previously just done handyman work. My dad had had dealings with him on jobs and thought he was a rough worker.
He thought everybody was rough, though.
To his credit, Dad was a very tidy worker. He always did a good job and always charged people according to what he thought they could afford.
Around fifteen, I started going out with Ken and a mutual friend. We often used to go to Ken's house after school.
Ken's house was utterly chaotic.
He had three younger sisters, aged between fourteen and six. All three girls were quite different. All great fun. Always laughing.
His mother was working away in the kitchen, cooking or washing. Us kids just played together. It was huge fun. His youngest sister once made us all laugh when she once put her whole fist in her mouth.
The toilet wasn't very clean. It was always brown with limescale, and often there was a large turd that didn't want to flush away lurking at the foot of the bend. I used to wee hard at it in an attempt to dislodge it.
On the sideboard in the living area was a small rectangular fish tank. The water in it was very murky and bright green. A solitary goldfish could occasionally be seen as it came close to the front.
Next to the tank, lounging on a pile of old women's magazines, the perpetually somnolent black kitten occasionally put its paw in the water in an attempt to touch the fish.
My mother really didn't like me going there, and I took to lying about where I was. I genuinely thought she was worried about nothing.
Over the next year, more and more of us ended up at Ken's after school. My mother knew I was there and got really sick of telling me not to go, so I stopped.
I think she was right. She just wanted me to concentrate on my exams and do well at school.
When I got my O Levels out of the way, I got a part-time job on an archaeological dig run by the DOE in a local old church and cemetery.
Ken was working there as well.
He told me that he'd been having problems with his dad. They'd got into a big fight one night and ended up throwing plates at one another in the kitchen. 
After that he said he'd moved into the shed down the garden. 
It sounded cold to me. 
He said it was fine. There was a big chest freezer in there and the back of it was really nice and warm. He said he'd been sleeping there for a year, from fifteen to sixteen.

When I started going to see him again after I was sixteen, he was back in the house, but living unconventionally, with a bed he'd built on top of a big wardrobe.

We soon got into a regular Saturday social round at Ken's: smoking fags and drinking Special Brew. My mother would have had a fit.
One afternoon, I noticed he'd also cut a hole in the ceiling.
When I asked him what it was, he said it was a private hatch he'd made so he could secretly build a room in the roof space. He told me to stick my head up and have a look.
It was quite impressive.
He'd been sneaking timber and tools up there when the rest of the house was empty or late at night when they’d all gone to bed.
Some months later, he got caught by one of his sisters, who shopped him to his dad.
Another huge fight ensued.
It was around then that my life went a bit awry. I had to drop out of the sixth form in the town and switch schools. 
This was at my mother's suggestion.
As usual, she was there to make the good decisions and get me back on track.
I lost touch with Ken again.
The next I heard, he'd emigrated to Australia and had been caught at Customs with a small amount of hash in his wallet that a mutual friend of ours had given him as a going-away present.
I thought about that a lot and it made me feel really uneasy. 
Many years later, I wondered what had happened to him. 
I found him quite quickly on Facebook and messaged him.
He'd moved to Western Australia, married an Australian woman and had a son. They lived in a small community near Perth.
Their boy was profoundly disabled, and Ken seemed really miserable and trapped by the situation.
We spoke a couple of times on Skype and then drifted apart again.
The year after, he messaged me and said he'd left the wife and kid in Australia and skipped to Germany. 
He was marrying a German woman and was now living in Cologne. I wondered about the morality of this for quite a while.
He asked me if he could stay with me for a night in London, where I was living then, on his way up to visit some mutual friends where we grew up.
I said that it would be great to catch up.
He parked his bike in the yard at the back of mine, and we sat up most of the night chatting.
As it had been on my mind, I apologised for the time I'd shopped him to the teacher over the computer.
He said he didn't remember.
He apologised to me for having pushed me over once when I was annoying him. I was really small for my age and had the mobility problems then which I still have.
I said I didn't remember that either, and we both laughed.
He went on his way the next day and stayed another night with me on his way back to Germany.
After that, we fell out of touch again.
He'll be back.
